 import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd

countries = [
    'Portugal', 'Poland', 'Mexico', 'Indonesia', 'Vietnam', 'Philippines', 'Colombia', 'Brazil'
]

sectors = {
    'Services': {
        'Formal': [51.3, 43.8, 40.1, 45.2, 13.2, 16.0, 19.8, 62.7],
        'Informal': [32.5, 38.6, 35.9, 30.8, 27.1, 45.3, 37.6, 28.4]
    },
    'Industry': {
        'Formal': [19.5, 23.4, 16.2, 22.7, 16.5, 13.0, 11.2, 20.3],
        'Informal': [14.2, 18.5, 27.6, 20.4, 26.9, 19.4, 23.8, 15.7]
    },
    'Agriculture': {
        'Formal': [11.3, 11.1, 8.9, 12.3, 2.8, 1.7, 5.9, 8.5],
        'Informal': [22.1, 19.7, 31.5, 35.2, 41.6, 32.0, 33.5, 25.3]
    }
}

unemployment_rate = [6.1, 3.4, 3.5, 4.2, 2.3, 5.3, 10.7, 9.3]
gdp_per_capita = [24000, 18000, 10500, 4800, 3700, 3800, 6600, 7500]
informal_share = [17.9, 21.7, 54.8, 50.3, 67.5, 69.3, 63.1, 42.8]

data = []
for sector, employment in sectors.items():
    for status, values in employment.items():
        for country, value in zip(countries, values):
            data.append({
                'Country': country,
                'Sector': sector,
                'Employment Type': status,
                'Employment Share (%)': value
            })

df_employment = pd.DataFrame(data)

df_economics = pd.DataFrame({
    'Country': countries,
    'Unemployment Rate (%)': unemployment_rate,
    'GDP per Capita (USD)': gdp_per_capita,
    'Informal Employment Share (%)': informal_share
})

plt.figure(figsize=(16, 12))
plt.suptitle("Sectoral Employment Distribution and Economic Indicators by Country (2023)",
             y=1.02, fontsize=16)

plt.subplot(2, 2, (1, 2))
sns.barplot(
    data=df_employment,
    x='Country',
    y='Employment Share (%)',
    hue='Sector',
    palette=['#4e79a7', '#f28e2b', '#59a14f'],
    dodge=False
)
plt.title("Employment Distribution by Sector (Formal vs Informal)")
plt.xlabel("Country")
plt.ylabel("Employment Share (%)")
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')
plt.legend(title='Sector', bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left')

for i, bar in enumerate(plt.gca().patches):
    if i % 3 == 1:
        bar.set_hatch('//')
    elif i % 3 == 2:
        bar.set_hatch('\\')

plt.subplot(2, 2, 3)
sns.barplot(
    data=df_economics,
    x='Country',
    y='GDP per Capita (USD)',
    color='#59a14f'
)
plt.title("Unemployment Rate (%)")
plt.xlabel("Country")
plt.ylabel("Unemployment Rate (%)")
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')

plt.subplot(2, 2, 4)
sns.barplot(
    data=df_economics,
    x='Country',
    y='Unemployment Rate (%)',
    color='#b07aa1'
)
plt.title("GDP per Capita (USD)")
plt.xlabel("Country")
plt.ylabel("GDP per Capita (USD)")
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("output.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
SUMMARY
 This image presents a detailed comparative analysis of sectoral employment distribution and key economic indicators across eight countries for the year 2023. The chart is divided into three distinct sections, each offering insights into different aspects of employment and economic performance.

The top section features a stacked bar chart illustrating the employment distribution by sector, differentiated between formal and informal employment types. The sectors are color-coded: blue for Services, orange for Industry, and red for Agriculture. Each bar represents a country—Portugal, Poland, Mexico, Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines, Colombia, and Brazil—showing the proportion of employment within each sector. The formal employment segments are solid, while the informal segments are marked with diagonal hatching. For instance, in Portugal, the Services sector has the largest share of employment (approximately 51.3% formal and 32.5% informal), whereas in Vietnam, Agriculture has a significant informal share (around 41.6%). Brazil displays a prominent formal Services sector, while the Philippines and Vietnam exhibit substantial informal employment in Agriculture.

The bottom left section is a bar chart depicting the unemployment rate by country. The bars, colored in green, reveal that Colombia has the highest unemployment rate at around 10.7%, while Vietnam has the lowest at approximately 2.3%. Other countries fall between these extremes, with Portugal at 6.1%, Poland at 3.4%, and Brazil at 9.3%, among others.

The bottom right section presents another bar chart, this time focusing on GDP per capita in USD, using purple bars. Portugal leads with the highest GDP per capita at about $24,000, followed by Poland with around $18,000. On the lower end, Vietnam and the Philippines have GDP per capita values close to $3,700 and $3,800, respectively. Colombia and Brazil have intermediate values, with Colombia around $6,600 and Brazil about $7,500.

Overall, this image provides a comprehensive view of the employment landscape and economic conditions across the selected countries, highlighting significant variations in sectoral employment distribution, unemployment rates, and GDP per capita.
